linkages: Self-reported demographics (nationality, tax registration form) linked to each courier's weekly working-time series by the platform's own encrypted courier ID.
No linkage to Danish national registers: 'This encryption prevented us from linking the data to individual background data on the couriers in national registers' (p. 7).
Platform policy automatically deletes user accounts inactive for several months, so a courier who left and re-entered the platform after a long absence cannot be linked across the gap (p. 15).

sample.universe: All food delivery couriers who worked for Wolt in Denmark between February 2017, when the platform started operating in Denmark, and the last week of 2022 (a full population of the platform's couriers, not a survey sample)
sample.unit_of_observation: courier-week (weekly online hours); couriers (weekly working-time sequences) are the units clustered into segments
selection_rules: Start from the full dataset of 20,090 individual courier trajectories on Wolt in Denmark, February 2017 - last week of 2022.

Exclude trajectories that began in the second half of 2022, because their limited duration (possibly continuing into 2023) would not permit meaningful longitudinal analysis and risked misclassification due to limited recorded activity.
This leaves 17,641 couriers analysed by weekly online hours.
In-house platform positions for employees such as developers or designers are excluded from the analysis (only self-employed 'courier partners' are studied).

For the demographic table (Table 5), restrict to the Regulars segment with non-missing self-reported nationality / tax registration: N = 1449 of 1679; missing values 1% (nationality) and 0.3% (tax registration). Demographics of Dabblers and Temporaries are not analysed because around 60% and 30% of values are missing.
sample.period: February 2017 - last week of 2022 (Figures 4 and 5 run February 2017 - June 2022)
sample.n_observations: not reported as a count of courier-weeks; 17,641 weekly working-time sequences over up to 6 years

construction_notes: 'Online hours' is a continuous weekly variable: the total hours per week a courier was logged onto the platform app, values between 0 and 126 hours. It includes non-delivery time such as waiting for incoming or delayed restaurant orders.

The continuous online-hours variable is coded into six weekly working time states (Table 2): Full-time +30; Long part-time 15-30; Short part-time 5-15; Few hours <5; Inactive 0 (on the platform but logging less than 2 hours); Not on platform (absent). The cut-points were partly inspired by Piasna et al. (2022) and Urzi Brancati et al. (2020).
Transition probabilities between the six states were computed across all 17,641 sequences (Table A1) and used to derive the substitution-cost matrix for optimal matching (Table A2).

Sequences were compared with the 'optimal matching' (OM) method in the R package TraMineR and clustered with Ward's method; cluster-number tests (two, three, four or more clusters), also re-run within individual calendar years, led to a three-cluster solution.
In Figures 1-3 all couriers' starting weeks (week 0) are aligned regardless of when they joined the platform, so the x-axis is weeks since entry rather than calendar time.
Figures 4 and 5 are in calendar time (February 2017 - June 2022) and decompose, respectively, total weekly online hours and weekly active couriers into the three segments.

The working time series includes numerous courier-weeks exceeding 100 online hours, which the authors read as evidence that the platform did not edit the data before transfer (couriers may remain logged on after work, or several couriers may share a profile).

key_assumptions.assumption: The weekly online-hours series supplied by the platform is unedited and complete for the couriers observed, i.e. the platform did not alter the data before transfer

key_assumptions.assumption: The analysed population is conditioned on having started on the platform before the second half of 2022: of the 20,090 individual courier trajectories, those beginning in the second half of 2022 were excluded because their limited duration risked misclassification, leaving 17,641
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 3.1: the authors state the exclusion and its rationale; no sensitivity analysis including these trajectories is reported

key_assumptions.assumption: Observed sequences are complete working histories: couriers who left and re-entered the platform after a long absence are treated as separate or truncated trajectories, because platform policy deletes accounts inactive for several months
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 5.2 'Limitations and future studies' states the account-deletion policy and that it made the authors unable to trace workers leaving and re-entering over longer periods; no correction is attempted

key_assumptions.assumption: Weekly online hours measure working time: the measure counts all hours logged onto the app, including waiting for incoming or delayed restaurant orders, and is taken to represent the courier's working time activity
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 3.1 states the construction and the caveat explicitly; no alternative measure is available in the data

key_assumptions.assumption: The three-cluster optimal-matching / Ward solution is the appropriate partition of the 17,641 weekly working-time sequences, and segment membership is treated as fixed and known in all downstream descriptives
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 3.4: tests of two, three and four-or-more cluster solutions using Ward's method on cluster consistency, theoretical interpretability and optimal matching, re-run within individual calendar years; two clusters gave asymmetric sequences and four or more gave very subtle differences

key_assumptions.assumption: Aligning every courier's first week on the platform at week 0 makes trajectories comparable irrespective of calendar date of entry, i.e. calendar-time effects are not confounded with time-since-entry in the segment descriptions
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 4 states the alignment; the paper gives no evidence that entry cohorts are comparable, and Section 4.1 shows platform conditions changed sharply over the period

key_assumptions.assumption: The six working-time states (+30 / 15-30 / 5-15 / <5 / inactive / not on platform) are the right discretisation of continuous weekly online hours, and the substitution-cost matrix derived from transition probabilities correctly prices dissimilarity between them
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 3.4 and Table 2; the cut-points are said to be partly inspired by Piasna et al. (2022) and Urzi Brancati et al. (2020); the cost matrix in Table A2 is calculated from the transition probabilities in Table A1

ambiguities: The schema's `sign` vocabulary has no value for a pure descriptive level. Convention used here: `sign` records the direction of the named group's value relative to the other groups printed in the same exhibit, as the paper itself orders them. The paper itself reports no contrast, test or interval. Dabblers are the lowest of the three printed segment means (9 vs 15.4 vs 24.2), and the paper calls the segment's activity 'limited'.
The paper does not say whether the segment mean is a mean over courier-weeks or a mean of courier-level means.

value.claimed_domain: The authors suggest the three working time segments appear both across different types of platforms and within specific gig work contexts; they also state that the longitudinal design 'may inform future studies of platform labor in similarly dynamic and less regulated contexts'.
boundary_conditions: generalizability is constrained by the platform-specific nature of the data; the studied platform represents a less restrictive algorithmic management regime allowing workers to accept and reject orders without penalties
gig platforms differ substantially in how they structure algorithmic management (task allocation, remuneration) and working conditions (task- or shift-based systems)
institutional factors such as national labor market regulations influence platform operations and workforce composition
